MONTREAL CANADA Jan. 10 th 1837. Further Particulars ofthelate Storm. þÿ 'I'he fourth north-easterly snow storm, since the 13th December, commenced on Sunday morning, about day-light, and continued till Monday night, whmi the wind changed to the westward, with continued snow, till about ton o'clock next morning. The quantity fallen is greater than is recollecrttd tor a very long period hack. It is probably from about eighteen inches to two feet on a level. The whole depth of snow fallen in the last eighteen days> is between four and live feet, where it did not drift. In the fields it is generally on a level with the tops of the fences. I he roads have become nearly impassable. '1 he Halifax mail, due on Monday morning, arrived only at ted yesterdav. It will be several davs before the roads w;!l admit of the arrival of the mail at the usual time. In the country paits around Quebec, the drilt, in consequence of the iiolenee of the wind, was so great as to prevent people from going to church, and the roads were not open tor sleighs up to last evening. In town, some houses were literally hurried under the snow, which was so high at several parts of the wall of the city, that a person on snow shoes might have walked over them, although they are between twenty and thirty feet in height.

The Legislature of the State of New York assembled at Albany on Tuesday last, the dav appointed by law, and organized by choosing Edwaro Livingston, Esqr. Speaker. On the same day, Governor Marcy sent down his annual message, which was read to the House by the Clerk. It occupies six columns of the Argus. This message, like the others which have emanated from the same source, is an able, statesmanlike document, and exhibits, in a clear and concise manner, the political and financial condition of the state, and the etfcct of various public measures, and their bearing u-jon the prosperity and well being ol the comnuniitv at large. Auer congratulating the Assembly on the triumph of democracy in the late Presidential Election, he alludes to the late law ofCongress for the distribution of the surplus revenue amona the States, in the form of loans or dcposites, to be returned when called for. By this law, the share which falls to the State of Mew York, is upwards of five millions of dollars. This he recommends to he funded, and the interest added to the school fund, for the support of schools. From this Message we learn that the number of organized school districts in the State, in 1835, was 10, þÿ 207. From 9,000 of these, reports have been received by the Superintendent. Rat Story. þÿ The following is a well authenticated fact, which occurred at Newburyport, Mass, upwards of five and forty years ago. A brig arrived in that port (from a foreign one) extremely invested with rats; the owners, after taking out the cargo, had her moored to the wharf, with planks leading to the shore ; a smoke was then made in the hold, which pervaded every part of the vesvel ; the rats took up their line of march for the shore, when, to the astonishment of the bvstanders. there appeared among them one which was infirm, blind, and white from age, holding in his mouth a stick, each end of which was. carried by another rat ! No consideration would have attempted us to hurt those three rats þÿ they sot so good an exam pie to our species.

JAMAICA. (From the Herald, December 7.) breach of privilege. There was a report in circulation yesterday evening, that Mr. Hyslop had made a motion in the House to bring up Mr. M'Qneen, for a breach ot privilege publishing in his refutation of the charges brought against Proprietors the and Directors of the Colonial Bank. The division on the motion had not taken place, when the gentleman from whom we received the statement left Spanish-Town. We are as anxious as any member of the House to preserve its privileges, and uphold the responsible and honorable character which it ought to

possess þÿ but we cannot see in what manner supposing the report to be true, placing Mr. M'Queen in custody of the Serjeant at arms, for refuting the calumnies of the interested, and discharging his duty to his constituents, can add either dignity or honour to the House. We shall no doubt be furnished with further particulars bv the two o'clock post, but as our paper goes to press about that hour, we are fearful we shall be unable to furnish further particulars to day. We understand that Mr. M'Queen has employed a short-hand writer to take minutes of the proceedings In that case, no doubt, the public will be put in possession of all the facts connected with this untoward arrest.

We have been kindly favoured bv a mercantile friend, with the following extract of a letter from Martinique, dated Nov. 16: þÿ " About one o'clock yesterday, a most melancholy circumstance happened, by which many lives were lost, some of them respectable characters. A warm spring having lately been discovered running between two high rocks in the heights near Precheur at the noi th end of the bay, whose medicinal property w as found to be a specific eleansieof cutanious disorders, has of late been much resorted to by all classes as a bathing place, who daily experienced its salutary effects From some cause not yet ascertained, but during a heavy roll of thunder in the mountains w ith rain, the bed of these rocks burst forth, bringing down snn df stones, and rocks of all sizes and descriptions, overwhelming every one within its influ r ce. Several bodies cut and mangled in a horrid manner have been got out, but many more are still supposed to be covered up; Madame I. arosiere wife of the Collector was one, her two children near the edge of the stream miraculously escaped þÿ an interesting young lady was so much disfigured that she could only be recognised by the ring on her finger. An examination has taken place, by which it appears a water spout had burst in the mountains. Several of the sufferers being relatives of principal families, has caused a deep and mournful sensation ; one poor girl was found covered up to the chin, and discovered to a person passing
some time after by her groans, she was dug out but 1 dont know if she will survive." þÿ Lhronicle December 13.

CURE FOR IRISH DISCONTENT. The author of a book called " Rambles on the Borders" thinks that Irish discontent and agitation are attributable more to their diet than any thing else. He savs. " It is evident that a people living on potatoe diet, and drinking whiskey, will necessarily become infiamable, and thus liable to be blown into a flame by the slightest breath of agitation. þÿ Were they to eat the bacon which they export, and to wash it down with a cup of ale, the sedative eliects ot this mode of living would be immediate apparent. Peep-of-days boys would no longer commit horrid murders at the noon of night, but would go to bed and sleep fiom 9 to 5, like decent Christian people; the White boys, now so gaunt and lean, would become sleek and rosy, and the occupation of Captain Rock, and Terry Alt, would be gone."

IMPORTANT. From the New York Express, Feb. 9, 1837. message op the president to the senate upon mexican affairs.

At the beginning of this session Congress was informed that our claims upon Mexico had not been adjusted, butthat notwithstanding the irritating effect upon her councils of the movements in Texas, I hoped by great forbearance to avoid the necessity of again bringing the subject of them to your notice. That hope has been disappointed Having in vain urged upon that Government the justice of these claims, and my indispensable obligation that there should be " no further delay the ac- in knowledgement, if not in the redress, of the injuries complained of," my duty requires that the whole subject should be presented' and now is, for the action of Congress, whose exclusive right it is to decide on the further measures of redress to he employed. The length of time since some of the injuries have been committed, the repeated and unavailing applications for redress, the wanton character of some of the outrages upon the property and persons of our citizens, upon the ffag of the United .States, independent of recent insults to this Government and People bv the late extraordinary Minister, would justify, in the/eyes of all nations, immediate war. That remedy, however, should not be used by just and generous nations, confiding in their strength, for injuries committed, if it can be honorably avoided, and it has occurred to me, that considering the present embarrassed condition of that country, we should act both with wisdom and moderation bv giving to Mexico one more opportunity to atone for the past,

before we take redress into our own hands þÿ To avoid all misconception on the part of Mexico, well to protect our own nation- as as al character from reproach, this opportunity should be given, with the avowed design and full preparation to take immediate satisfaction' if it should not be obtained on a repetition of the demand lor it. To this end, I recommend that an act be passed, authorizing reprisals, and the use of the naval force of the United States by the Executive against Mexico, to enforce thein in the event of a refusal by the Mexican Government to come to an amicable adjustment of the matters in controversy betweeu us, upon another demand thereof made from on board one of our vessels of war on the coast of Mexico. The Documents herewith transmitted, with others sent to the House of Representatives heretofore, will enable Congress to judge of the propriety of the course pursued, and to decide upon the necessity of that now recommended. If these views should fail to meet the concurrence of Congress, and that body be able to find in the condition of the affairs between the two countries, as disclosed by the accompanying documents, with those referred to, any well-grounded reasons to hope that an adjustment of the controversy between them, can be effected without a resort to the measures I have felt it my duty to recommend, they may be assured of my co-operat'on in any other course that shall be deemed honorable and proper. ANDREW JACKSON. Washington, Feb. 0, 16.17.
This message was referred to the Committee, on Foreign Relation.

IN SENATE þÿ Saturday, Jan. 25. The Vice President, after the reading of the Journal, addressed the Senate as follows:

Senators : The period is at hand which is to terminate the official relation which has existed between us, and 1 leave, probably never to return to it, a body with which 1 have been long connected ; where some remain whom I found here fiften years ago, and where in the progress of public duties, personal associations have arisen never to be forgotten. From such scenes I cannot retire without emotion. Nor can 1 give to the Senate the usual opportunity of choosing another to preside for a time over their deliberations, without referring to the manner in which I have endeavored to discharge a most gratifying and honorable trust connected with the office to which my country called me. Entering upon it with unaffected diffidence, well knowing how little my studies had been directed to its peculiar duties, I was yet strengthened by the determination then expressed, so to discharge the authority with which I was invested, rrs " best to protect the rights, to respect the feelings, and guard the reputations of all who would be affected by its exercise." 1 was sure that if successful in this, 1 should be pardoned for errors which I could hardly expect to avoid. In the interval that has since elapsed it has been our lot in this assembly to pass through scenes of unusual excitements; the intense interest on absorbing topics, which lias pervaded our whole community, could not be unfelt within these walls. The warmth of political parties, natural in such times, the ungual ded ardor of sudden debate, and the

collisions seldom to be separated from the invaluable privilege of free discussion, have not been unfrequently mingled with the more tranquil tenor of ordinary legislation. 1 cannot hope that, in emergencies like these, 1 have always been so fortunate as to satisfy every one around me ; yet, 1 permit myself to think that the extent to whicli my decisions have been approved by the' Senate is some evidence that my efforts justly to administer their rules have not been vain ; and I conscientiously cherish the conviction, that on no occasion have I departed from my early resolution, or been regardless of what was due to the rights or the feelings of the members of this body. 1 hough I may henceforth be separated from the Senate, I can never cease to revert with peculiar interest to my long connexion with it. In every situation in my future life 1 shall remember with a just pride the evidences of approbation and confidence which I have here received ; and as an American citizen, devotedly attached to the institutions of my country, 1 must always regard with becoming and sincere respect a branch of our Government, invested with such extensive powers, and designed by our forefathers to accomplish such important results. Indulging an ardent wish that every success may await you in performing the exalted and honorable duties of your public trust, and offering my warmest prayers that prosperity and happiness may be constant attendants on each of you, along the future paths of life, I
respeclluily bid you farewell.

The Duke of Wellington having been applied to relative to the distress of two ladies, the sisters of the late Lieut.-Colonel Hamilton, who was killed at Waterloo, returned the following letter : þÿ " Sir, þÿ I have the honour of receiving your letter, regarding the sisters of the late Col. Hamilton, of the Scots Greys. If I bad this single case to deal with, or a hundred, or even hundreds, I should be under no difficulty ; but, as soon as the war was over, nothing would avail the officers of the army, their relatives and relics, but exorbitant profits and interest. Instead of placing their money in security, and being satisfied with small, but secure, interest for the same they entrusted it to gamblers and speculators, whether in the profession of the law or otherwise, in order to acquire more than could be fairly made by money ;and the tale of distress, which you relate of the Misses Hamilton, is that not of hundreds, but, to my certain knowledge, of thousands All these naturally come to me from all parts of the world. I have, at this moment, applications before tne from Canada and the East Indies, as well as from different parts of Europe, and 1 must add, the relicts of officers of the army are not the only sufferers. The Government will do nothing, and 1 confess ihat I cannot see on what ground a grant of money can be justified, founded on losses ot fortune, occasioned by imprudent and unreasonable speculations. No private funds can provide for such demands 1 make this statement in answer to your letter,

as I wish to show that the case is not singular, at the same time, 1 send you the inclosed, requesting you will add to it any subscription which may have been made for the service of these ladies. I have the honour to be, vour must obedient humble servant, " Wellington."

the effects of revolutions in france. (F, am the Morning Herald,) " Young France." baptized in the blood of a recent revolution, displays all the unsteadiness þÿ the love of change þÿ the irregular impulses that are natural to the season of youth. Never was there a nation ie9s instructed by melancholy experience, or that derived less wisdom from adversity. For " young France,' ages of national history have been acted and written in vain. At this day the real liberty which France enjoys is certainly not more, if it be not less' than she possessed before her last revolution The ordinances of Charles X. were undoubtedly gross violations of the Charter. The laws which the Doctrinaire Ministers of Louis Philip passed, under pretext of the Fieschi plot, were all indefensible infringements of the public liberty, which the Charter had guaranteed; yet " young France" contin" ued with truiy juvenile ardour to celebrate the anniversary of tiie " three glorious days'' of winch the Fieschi laws were the fruit, and to worship the outward form of that liberty from which, in the moment of gaining it, life had departed of 1830 may now be described as the anarchy of three days, and the absolutism of six years. The people who had courage to achieve a great victory had not the wisdom to make a right use of it The State is in that condition in which a cor. rupt Lxecutive is surpassed in corruption by the legislative body. W hen the people were clamouring for the abolition of the hereditary

Peerage, they would have been more wisely j employed endeavouring in to obtain an enlargement of the representative system; indeed, they ought to have been made that a condition of the new settlement of the Crown. Less than half the number of electors which returned tbe British House of Commons before the Reform Bill, return the French Chamber of Deputies, and that for a nation which contains about thirty six millions of people. The hereditary House of Peers has been abolished, and what has the nation gained by it? 1 he Peers are now more cot ruptly subservient to the Crown than ever, and naturally enough. All independence was destroyed by the law which confiscated the inheritance of their honours, and they were compelled to become the servile tools of the Minister of the day, that the titles which perished with them, might be revived in their children. þÿ Thus, honours are to he purchased for the children only by the father's corrupt submission to the Minister; and this was clamoured for, and obtained, by the thoughtless people, as a reform and purification of the Peerage. In England, what would he thought of the administration of justice, if commoners accused of high treason could be arraigned at the bar of a Criminal Court, of which the J udges

and the Jury were one and the same bodyboth being Peers, but not the peers of the accused þÿ mongrel Nobles, entirely dependent the Crown for the reversion of their honours to their descendants, and consequently identified in feeling an interest with the prosecutor, who demanded at their hands the lives of the accused. Well might such a mode of trial be called the proces monstre ! It shows that France, whose centralizing system our Whig Reformers are most desirous to r.opyt is some centuries behind England in the practice and perception of Constitutional law. %

Government in "young France," since the three glorious days, has been almost a series of emeutes, intermixed with some more terrible commotions, such as, for instance, the barricade slaughter of the 5th and 6th of June in Paris, and the revolt and horrible carnage of Lyons. Many of the plots þÿ by the explosion of which the French nation, during the last six years, have been made dreadfully familiar with such occurrences þÿ afforded in themselves pretty strong circumstantial evidence of having been concocted by the agents of the central police system, or fomented by its spies, for of such a system espionage in its worst features is a necessary concomitant. # #

Whether the late abortive explosion of a ridiculous plot at Strasburg, has any thing to do with the plot, of which Conseil was tbe instrument, and which was concocted to afford a pretext for depriving Switzerland of her national independence, it is difficult to say ; but it is made use of by the French Government to justify its insolent attacks upon the independence of the Swiss nation, and to help itself out of the disgrace of the detected iniquity of the Conseil affair. Whether a giddy and hot heated young man, like Louis Napoleon, has deen decoyed from Switzerland by another Conseil to lake a part in a drama, of which the puppets were worked and the strings pulled at a place remote from Stras. burg, and whether the simultaneous and equally contemptible ebullition at Vcndome was of a similar character and origin, we pretend not to say. We know that the Doctrinaire Ministers have a great capacity for small things, and that political morality is at a considerable discount among Frenc h Stall s- ( man. Those who confidently assert that the I young member of the Buonaparte family was decoyed into a trap, expressly set lor him, may have more knowledge on the subject than we can pretend to have. At present the matter appears to us to be involved in an obscurity which it is not easy to penetrate. We hope, however, that a forfeiture of his life will no1 be exacted in a country where mercy lias been extended to the prisoners of Ham. From whatever causes they arise, frequency of plots, emeutes, and commotions in Fiance

indicate a very distempered state of the body politic, lt is a dangerous policy which makes things familiar to the public mind. þÿ What have the incessant prosecutions against the Fress done for the security of the French King's throne? What stability does public order receive from the centralizing system of Government, seeing that it is continually disturbed by such convulsive alarms? The result of these and other considerations is to make us more than ever prefer the free Constitution of Old England to the " liberties of July," and the centralized Government of" young France." þÿ þÿ r-czs<3 cjscy Printed and Published by RICHARD llATCUETT

dreaded foe, and the dazzling lustre of the Sicilian eye of beauty, with its flashing glances of approval, caused a palpitation even in mv young heart The Royal standard seen in the Admirals' barge, and the long measured stroke of the rowers, with the respectful standing position of the Lieutenant at the helm, denote that the very highest in the realm are on board. The boatswain's shri I pipe called attention ; and the words, ' All hands man ship ahov I" re echoed by his mates through the different decks, instantly placed eight hundred men in our rigging, the light topmen, that were to ascend the dizz\ heights of the Royal yards, in advance. The band played a march, the guard presented arms, and the Olficers uncovered,

as the descendant of Maria Theresa placed her foot on the deck of the conqueror's ship. The Sicilian Royal standard superceded Lord Nelson's flag, and the unfolding of its banners roused the sleeping thunder of the squadron. A Royal salute welcomed this energetic woman, whose slender and perfect form seemed to tread on air, while the tender animation of her sparkling eyes expressed a warmth of heart that prompted her (at least in my imagination) to embrace all around her. Very little time did she devote to the splendid collation prepared for her þÿ but, with her amiable daughters, sought to soothe the anguish of pain, and alleviate the sufferings of tiie wounded. This youthful garb my eagerness bespeaks, This morning cap proclaims my lengthened years And many a wrinkle in my grief-worn cheeks, Hath oft been met with disappointment's tears.

Yon ball, for which I a sovereign paid, So tempting, balked my wishes at the last, Through Weipport there the music had purveyed. And Gunter a magnificent repast. Hard is the fate of maids no longer young! Deaf to my hints were all the dancing men 1 And envying in my heart the blooming throng, I waltzed with partners of three þÿ score and ten ! Oh let me but avoid the wretched doom, Which menaces old maids, as gossips tell, When they have passed the precints of the tomb. To lead the apes they loved on earth, in hell !

Should I reveal the scources of my grief, If soft humanity 'er touched their breast, Sure bachelors could not withhold relief! And pitying offers would not be represt ! Heaven sends us offers ! why should we refuse ? 'Tis that has brought me to the state you see ; And should they hesitate too long to choose, Young ladies soon will grow old maids like me 1
A little beauty once I had to boast, Then sprightly as a sylph 1 hailed the hall ; But ah ! too soon I ceased to reign a toast, And rival belles delighted in my fall.
My sister once the comfort of my youth, Luted by an oliering from her native halls, Now lives confiding in a husbands truth, While in her nursery many an infant squalls !
My lover once ! sweet soother of my cares ! Struck by consumption, at death's stern decree, A victim fell to brandy and cigars, And left the world to wretchedness and me !

UNLAWFUL WEAPONS. (From the Philadelphia Sentinel.) In no part of the civilized world does the practice of carrying deadly weapons prevail so extensively as in the United States. þÿ Throughout the southern and western States, almost every man is armed with a pistol, a dirk, a Bowie knife, a sword caneor a bullet headed rattan ; and we regret that truth compels us to add, this highly reprehensible practice is rapidly increasing in the middle and northern States. On no ground can this practice be defended ; but very substantial reasons can be assigned for prohibiting it þÿ and we do not hesitate to say that it ought to be severely prohibited in every State in the Union þÿ Startling as the assertion may seem, we are confident it is susceptible of proof that among the sixteen millions which constitute the population of the United States, more homicides and felonious assaults are committed in one year than among any thirty millions of people of Christian Europe, in time of peace, in two years. Why should this be, unless the practice of carrying deadly weapons be the principal cause ! It is certain that when a man is armed with a pistol or a knife, he is much disposed to use it in a quarrel ; and if his adversary be armed also, his weapons will be drawn in self defence, and a homicide or attempt at one will always infallibly ensue. Besides, a man thus armed is much more disposed to quarrel Conscious of his strength in deadly weapons, he is more ready both to give and take offence. We talk much about

the assassinations of Spain and Italy ; about the murderous knife of the one, and the treacherous stiletto of the other We believe that more cases of stabbing occur in New Y'ork or Philadelphia in one year, than in Rome or Naples or iMadrid or Lisbon in five. The reason usually assigned for carrying deadly weapons, is self dejrnce. Against whom or w hat ? Against ruffians and assassins, who are generally armed with these severe weapons. But would not those who assign this reason, argue more legically by saying that this practice produces ruffians and assassius, and that the best defence against them was not to imitate their pernicious example, but to take from them, by law, the means of indulging their ferocious propensity ? The practice belongs to a cowardly, perfidious people, and is altogether unworthy of those who profess to be civilized, and to be governed by laws. The southern people, among whom this practice prevails far more extensively than among us of Pennsylvania, boast greatly of their chivalry and high sense of honour Yet in the days of chivalry, this practice was entirely unknown. þÿ Knights and chevaliers were always armed, but never with concealed weapon. The lance and sword were their weapons, to be used only in fair combat, never in secret murder or ruffian brawls. Dirks, pistols and sword canes are the appropriate instruments of assassination þÿ of cowardly, secret murder. In England, the carrying of unlawful weapons is forbidden bv severe laws. Hence the

rarity of homicide or maiming in quarrels in that country. Murders occur in England as in all countries, but assassination is by no means a characteristic of the people. On the contrary, they are remarkable for a tnanlv and ingenuous abhorrence of such practices, whi !» they denounce as the vices of a cowardly p(><» t a ecn produced by their severe lawr le. The other puffed up with pride, affected not to know his visitor, and inquired who he was, and why he came there. " Then you do not recognise me ?" said the man, mortified ; " I am your old friend ; I heard you had become blind, and I came to ascertain if it was true : 1 see it is so, and I am surry for it "

A person, who had contracted an intimacy with a miser, said to him one day ; " I am about to make a journey ; give me your ring; 1 will preserve it carefully, and when I look at it I shall think of you " The miser replied ; " If you wish to think of me you had better look at your finger, and then you will remember having asked me for the ring, and I refused to give it you."

Our readers will be glad to learn the question of communication with India, by the agency of steam power, has at last assumed a shape that cannot fail to bring this long talked of, and earnestly desired, object into immediate operation. We have always been deeply impressed with its importance ; but if we had not, the conviction would have forced itself upon us at this moment, while we are perusing the document upon our table þÿ we allude to a prospectus that is now being circulated amongst the mercantile interests ol this country. It will be remembered we have before declared the promoters of this undertaking were backed by the most influential, as well as by the general interests of this city, and that o' the manufacturing and provincial towns of the kingdom connected with the India trade. þÿ We were not, however, prepared to see it supported to the extent and strength it has reached, and with so little notice of its circulation. When we know that sums averaging from two to five thousand pounds have been readily subscribed by different firms for the purchase of stock in the proposed " East India Steam Navigation Company," it is the best warrantly the public can have of the sound policy of the measure, and of its great practical utility. There is another feature in this document that at once stamps it with an honesty of purpose, and places the object beyond even the suspicion of its being either a bubble or a job. Contrary to the usual style so much in fash-

ion at the present day, when the public are invited to become shareholders in a company, this prospectus sets forth a statement, showing that a grand scale of usefulness is contemplated and expected rather than inordinate profits, while it appears to be a legitimate investment for all those interested in its well-doing' by whom it will and ought to he supported ; thus began, it is clear, when the measure shall he perfected and have come into full and steady work, it will he an outlay producing to the stockholders a fair and adequate remuneration. We are free to confess the benefits this undertaking is calculated to bestow have never hitherto been demonstrated to the extent that is so forcibly thrust upon us by the details we are now looking at, and when we see so clear a way of approximating England, we may say Europe, to those distant parts of the globe, how flimsy and untenable appear all the objections that have hitherto been urged to prevent this sceme being carried into execution. India, China, and Austialia are all within the easy grasp of this comprehensive plan, and it is fair to suppose the latter will follow on the line of the India route, as that the railroad will he continued from Manchester to Bermingham, and who doubts that? Assuming this extended operation to take place, we must bear in mind the whole line of sea from Ceylon to Australia is particularly well adapted for steam navigation ; and moreover, when we see the daily improvements that are taking place in the marine steam en-

gine, there can he no doubt the times estimated will be materially shortened, perhaps onethird ; þÿ at present they are as follows : þÿ Falmouth to Cadiz and Gibraltar, f> days; Malta, 14 days ; Alexandria, 10 days; Bombay, 48 days; Madras, 55 days; Calcutta, 50 days ; I'enung, 57 days ; Sineapose, (!0 days ; Battavia, (52 days ; Australia, 73 days; Canton, 08 days ; Mauritius, 54 days.

We have watched this measure with great interest, and shall continue to do so, quite assured it will he productive of great blessings to a large portion of mankind ; the work is in good hands, and when they are ready to make a fair stand there can he no doubt but the Kings Government, in the true spirit of doing signal service, will be quite ready, and accede to the reasonable demands that have been made. þÿ A aval and Military Gazette.

The editor of the New York Express, noticing the amount of business transacted in the commercial whirlpool, and its prospective prosperity, thus speaks of the never ending bustle : " There are no moments for recereation, no day for rest, no time for pauses, and but few hours for reflection. If, reader, you doubt what we say, go with us through Nassau street or Wall street at midnight. The very ground under you shall shake and tremble like an earthquake with the artillery of the press, and upon every side you can see not/ling hut the sky above you, which gives even the appearance of night. Go too, through Broadway, along the Park, and by the Bowery, and nothing hut the illuminations that surround you, will whisper that night has succeeded day. Thus it is with us þÿ day and night, night and day. Men here walk faster, talk taster, think faster, eat faster, drink faster, and sleep faster, than any where else. Speed is written upon every thing from the pulpit to the press, and from the press to the workshop. The age of poetry, of music, of fancy, of beauty, and of goods is all ideal with us, or with the male portion of us at least þÿ and instead of it we have the age of business, of velocity, of enterprise and excitement. Nothing frightens us or impedes our progress. Fires and accidents are expected as a matter of course. The destruction of millions of dollars upon land or sea excite no alarm and create no surprise. T welve-months sTnee and the wealthier part of the city was in flames and in

ruins. The alarm was but momentary ; fear soon subsided, and danger was over. Like practical common sense men, instead of mourning over their losses, the losers immediately commenced gathering up their fortunes, and by deligence and industry were again upon the road to wealth and prosperity. Not a failure followed ; no distrust was created in the minds of any one ; and now it would seem from the beauty, present and promising and compactness, where once all was different, that our greatest calamity would prove our greatest blessing Such is the enterprise of our great and magnificent city, which is known, and well known, over almost the entire world þÿ such too, is the city which is destined in time to outstrip in wealth, in commerce, in influence and in population, the greatest cities of the world.

BIRTH EXTRAORDINARY. From the Standard. An event interesting to physiologists occurred at half past six o'clock on Sunday morning. The wife of the dwarf, Don Santiago de los Santos (herself a dwarf,) was delivered of a well-formed male infant, at their residence No. 167, High Holborn near Museum-Street The accouchers were Mr. Bowden, of Sloane Street Chelsea (who once before attended Santiago on a similar occasion,) and Dr. Davis of Saville row. Both gentlemen had for some time been very assiduous in their attentions to the little Lady ; but the infant though it came into the world alive did not survive its birth above an hour. Its length is 1 3 inches and a half ; its weight is one pound four ounces and a half (a vordupois) ; it is in every respect well formed It was carried in a coffin to St George's Church, Blooms bury ; but, being there refused sepulture, it was taken home, preserved in spirits, and will be exhibited for some time, previously to being deposi ted in one of our public museums. Dr. Davis was very anxious to have it submitted to dissection, and to lecture upon it, at the theatre of the London University ; this, however, was declined by the Lilliputian parents, who appear to feel poignantly this second disappointment of their hopes. It will be recollected that the father is the same iSpanish dwarf who made complaint before the Lord Mayor some time ago, of having been robbed by one of his countrymen of his savings, which had been deposited in the public funds. Don Santiago, who is only 25 inches high,

is at present in his 50th year. He is a native of the Spanish settlement of Manilla; in one of the forests of which, it seems, he was exposed to death in his infancy, on account of hrs diminutive size. He was however miraculously saved by the Viceroy, who, happening to be hunting in that quarter, humanely ordered him to be taken care of. His parents, who were afterwards discovered, were farmers, and were, with their other children (sons and daughters) of robust frame, and rather above the usual height. When he was 20 years of age, his humane protector, the Viceroy, died, and attachment to the land of his birth to

(which he often sav s he will return) prevented him from accompanying his foster brothers and sisters to Old Spain. Neglected by his own parents and family, he suffered hardships and privations of the most afflicting nature. At length he found his way to Madras, and was, about six years ago brought to England by the captain of a trading vessel. During tho voyage he was washed overboard by a heavy sea, but hen coops and spars being thrown out and other assistance afforded, his life was saved On his arrival in northern latitudes' he suffered severely from cold, and even now' though inured to t he climate he cannot swallow cold water. Still, he never goes near a fire, although he feels sensibly if his room be not kept warm, lie is stoutly built, and generally possesses cheerful spirits and good health. His habits are moderate, seldom drinking any thing but warm water ; but, on his birih days wedding anniversaries, and other festivals, he indulges in a few glasses of wine ; and does the other honours of the table with much dignity, hospitality, and eclat. He is fond of music; but his ruling passion appears to be a fondness for gay and glittering attire, jewellery and silver plate, to all which luxuries he had been accustomed. His mind appears to be impressed with the tenets of the Catholic Church, in which his foster father took care to have him duly instructed. He reads his prayer-book and psalter every morning and evening, very devoutly crossing himself, and performing his genuflections, with nil the other

ceremonies inculcated by the teachers of that faith. Besides his native tongue, he speaks an Indian patois, converses freely in Portuguese, and in English indifferently well. He became acquainted with his little wife at Birmingham, of which town she is a native. Her name was Ann Hopkins, and lier height 38 inches, being 13 inches taller than himself. She is 31 years of age, and possesses much symmetry and grace. Her lather stands sir feet, one inch and a half, without his shoes : her mother is of middle size : and her brothers and sisters (of whom they are nine in all) are tall and robust. The little Don and Donna live together very affectionately, their attachment having been mutual, and at first sight ; the only difference of opinions, that she being a Protestant, they do not worship together; and tliat ever since the attempted robbery of her husband by his countrymen, she hates all Spaniards, and pouts and frets and scolds whenever she sees him converse with one They were married on the 6th of July, 1834, in the Catholic Chapel at Barmingham, and two days after at St. Martin's Church in the same town, by the Rev. Mr, Fove, the high bailiff giving the bride away.

From the New York Evening Star, March 6. INAUGURAL ADDRESS. Fellow Citizens: The practice of all my predecessors imposes on me an obligation 1 cheerfully fulfil, to accompany the first and solemn act of my pub lie trust with an avowal of the principles that will guide me in performing it, and an expression of my feelings on assuming a charge so responsible and vast. In imitating their example, I tread in the footsteps of illustrious men, whose superiors, it is our happiness to believe, are not found on the executive calen dar of any country. Among them, we recognise the earliest and firmest pillars of the republic; those by whom our national independence was first declared þÿ him who, above all others, contributed to establish it on the field of battle ; and those whose expanded intellect and patriotism constructed, improved, and perfected the inestimable institutions under which we live. If such men, in the position i now occupy, felt themselves overwhelmed by a sense of gratitude for this, the highest of all marks of their country's confidence, and by a consciousness of their inability adequately to discharge the duties of an office so difficult and exalted, how much more must these considerations affect one, who can rely on no such claims for lavor or forbearance. Unlike all who have preceded me, the revolution, that gave us existence as a antion, was achieved at the period of my birth ; and whilst 1 contemplate with grateful reverence that memorable event, I feel that I belong to a later age, and that 1 may not expect my coun

trymen to weigh my actions with the same kind and partial hand. So sensibly, fellow citizens, do these circumstances press themselves upon me, that I should not dare to enter upon mv path of duty, did 1 not look for the generous aid of those who will be associated with me in the various and co-ordinate branches of the Government ; did I not repose, with unwavering reliance, on the patriotism, the intelligence, and the kindness, of a people who never yet deserted a public servant honestly laboring in their cause; and, above all, did I not permit myselfhumblv to hope for the sustaining support of an everwatchful and beneficent Providence. To the confidence and consolation derived from these sources, it would be ungrateful not to add those which spring from our present fortunate condition. Though not altogether exempt from embarrassments that disturb our tranquility at home and threaten it abroad, yet, in all the attributes of a great, happy, and flourishing people, we stand without a parallel in the world. Abroad, we enjoy the respect, and, with scarcely an exception, the friendship of every nation : at home, while our Government quietly, but efficiently, performs the ole legitimate end of political institutions, in doing the greatest good to the greatest number, we present an aggregate of human prosperity surely not elsewhere to be found. How imperious, then, is the obligation imposed upon every citizen, in his own sphere of action, whether limited or extended, to exert

himself in perpetuating a condition of things so singularly happy. All the lessons of history and experience must be lost upon us if we are content to trust alone to the peculiar advantages we happen to possess Position and climate, and the bounteous resources that nature has scattered with so liberal a hand even the diffused intelligence and elevated

TSsvximisR &a<Mn&&xrM A<T:IS character of our people þÿ will avail us nothing, if we fail sacredly to uphold those political institutions that were wisely and deliberately formed, with reference to every circumstance that could preserve, or might endanger, the blessings we enjoy. The thoughtful framers of our constitution legislated for our country as they found it Looking upon it with the eyes of statesmen and of patriots, they saw all the sources of rapid and wonderful prosperity ; but they saw also that various habits, opinions, and institutions, peculiar to the various portions of so vast a region, were deeply fixed. Distinct sovereignties were in actual existence, whose coiuial union was essential to the welfare and happiness of all. Between many of them there was at least to some extern, a real diversity of interests, liable to be exaggerated through sinister designs ; they differed in size, in population, in wealth, and in actual and prospective resouices and power ; tliey varied in the cfiaiacter of their industry and staple productions ; and in some existed domestic institutions, which, unwisely disturbed, might endanger the harmony of the whole. Most careiully were all these circumstances weighed and the foundations of the new Government laid upon principles of recipocal concession and equitable compromise. The jealousies which the smaller States might entertain of the power of the rest were allayed by a rule of representation, conlessedly unequal at the time, and designed forever to re-

main so. A natural fear that the broad scope of general legislation might bear upon and unwisely control particular interests, was counteracted by limits strictly drawn around the action of the feueral authority ; and to the people and the States was left unimpaired their sovereign power over the iniiuiiieiable subjects embraced in the internal government of a just republic, excepting such only necessarily appertain as to the concerns of tne whole confederacy, or its intercouise, as a united community, with the other nations of the world. This provident forecast has been verified by time. Half a century, teeming with extraordinary events, and elsewhere producing astonishing results, has passed along ; but on our institutions it has left no injurious mark. þÿ From a small community, we have risen to a people powerful in numbers and in strength ; but with our increase has gone, hand in hand, the progress of just principles ; the privileges, civil and religious, of the humblest individual are still sacredly protected at home ; and, while the valor and fortitude of our people have removed lar from us the slightest apprehension of foreign power, they have not yet induced us, in a single instance, to forget what is right. Our commerce has been extended to the remotest nations : the value, and even nature of our productions has been greatly changed > a wide difference has arisen in the relative wealth anu resources of every portion of our country ; vet the spirit of mutual regard and

ol faithful adherence to existing compacts, has continued to prevail in our councils, and never long been absent from our conduct. We have learned by experience a fruitful lesson ; that an implicit and undeviating adherence to the principles on which we set out, can carry us prosperously onward through all the conflicts of circumstances, and the vicissitudes inseparable from the lapse of years. The success that has thus attended our great experiment, is, in itself, a sufficient cause for gratitude, on account of the happiness it has actually conferred, and the example it has

unanswerably given. But to me, my fellow citizens, looking forward to the far-distant future( with ardent prayers and confiding hopes, this retrospect presents a ground for still deeper delight. It impresses on my mind a firm belief that the perpetuity of our institutions depends upon ourselves ; that, if we maintain the principles on which they were established, they are destined to confer their benefits on countless generations yet to come ; and that America will present to every friend of mankind the cheering proof, that a popular Government wisely formed, is wanting in no element of endurance or strength. Fifty years ago, its rapid failure was boldly predicted. Latent and uncontrollable causes of dissolution were supposed to exist, even by the wise and good ; and not only did unfriendly or speculative theorists anticipate for us the fate of past republics, but the lears of many an honest patriot overbalanced his sanguine hopes. Look back on these forebodings, not hastily, but reluctantly made, and see how, in every instance, they have completely failed. And imperfect experience, during the struggles of the revolution, was supposed to warrant a belief that the people would not bear the taxation requisite to discharge an immense public debt already incurred, and to defray the necessary expenses of the Government. þÿ The cost of two wars has been paid, not only without a murmur, but with unequalled alacrity. .No one is now left to doubt that every burden will be cheerfully borne that may be

ncccssuiy to sustain our civil institutions, or guard our honor or our welfare. Indeed, all experience has shown that the willingness of the people to contribute to these ends in cases of emergency, (has uniformly outrun the confidence ol ifieir representatives. In the early stages ol the new Government, when ail felt the imposing influence, as tliey recognised the unequalled services of the first President, it was a common sentiment that the great weight of his character could alone bind the discordant materials of our Government together, and save us from the violence of contending factions. Since his death, nearly forty years are gone, l'arty exasperation has been often carried to its highest point ; the virtue and the lorlitude of the people have sometimes been greatly tried : yet our system, purified and enchanced in value by all it has encountered, still preserves its spirit of free and fearless discussion, blended with unimpaired fraternal feeling. The capacity of the people for self-government, and their w illingness, from a high sense ot duty, and without those exhibitions of coercive power so generally employed in other countries, to submit to all needful restraints and exactions of the municipal law, have also been favorably exnrnplified in the history of the American States. Occasionally, it is true, the ardor of public sentiment, outrunning the regular progress of the judicial tribunals, or seeking to reach causes not denounced as criminal by the existing law, has displayed itself

in a manner calculated to give pain to the friends of free government, and to encourage the hopes of those who wish for its overthrow. These occurrences, however, have been far less frequent in our country than in any other of equal population on the globe ; and with the diffusion of intelligence, it may well be hoped that they will constantly diminish in frequency and violence. The generous patriotism and sound common sense of the great mass of our fellow citizens, will assuredly, in time, produce this result; for as every assumption ol illegal power not only wounds the

majesty of the law, but furnishes pretext a for abridging the liberties of the people, the latter have the most direct and permanent interest in preserving the great land marks of social order, and maintaining, on all occasions, the inviolability of those constitutional and legal provisions which thev themselves have made. In a supposed unfitness of our institutions for those hostile emergencies, which no country can always avoid, their friends found a fruitful source of apprehension, their enemies of hope. While they foresaw less promptness of action than in Governments differently formed; they ovei looked the far more important consideration that with us war could never be the result of individual or irresponsible will, but must be a measure of redress for injuries sustained, voluntarily resorted to by those who were to bear the necessary sacrifice, who would consequently feel an individual interest in the contest, and whose energy would be commensurate with the difficulties to be encountered. Actual events have proved their error ; the last war, far from impairing, gave new confidence to our Government ; and amid recent apprehensions of a similar conflict, we saw that the energies of our country would not be wanting in ample season to vindicate its rights. We may not possess, as we should not desire to possess, the extended and ever ready military organization of other nations ; we may occasionally suffer in the outset for the want of it ; but, among ourselves,
all doubt upon this great point has ceased, while a salutary experience will present a contrary opinion from inviting aggression from abroad. (To be concluded in our next )

We understand the following directions and instructions, for the information of all sailors who may he inclined to trip it, as all sailors from time immemorial are wont, on the light fantastic toe, were recently found amongst the papeis of the late Sir Joseph Yorke, of facetious memory. FIRST FIGURE. Le Pantalon. þÿ Haul upon the starboard tack, let the other craft pass, then bear up and get your head on the other tack, regain your berth on the larboard tack, back and fill with your partner, box-haul her, wear round twice against the sup, in company with the opposite craft and your own ; afterwards box haul her again, and bring up. SECOND FIGURE. þÿL Ete þÿ Shoot a-head about two fathoms till you nearly come stern on the other craft Under weigh; then make a stern bound to your berth, side out for a bend, first to starboard and then to port, make sail and pass the other craft, get your head round on the other tack, another bend to starboard and port, make sail to regain your berth, wear round, back and fill, and box haul your partner, and heave to. THIRD FIGURE La Poule. þÿ Heave ahead and pass vour adversary yard arm and yard arm, regain your berth on the other tack ; in the same

order take your station in the line with your partner, back and fill, fall on your heel and bring up with your partner ; she then manoeuvres ahead, heaves all aback, shoots ahead again, and pays off along side ; you then make sail in company with her till nearly stern with the other line; make a stern board, and cast her off to shift for herself; regain vour berth by the best means in your power, and let go your anchor. FOURTH FIGURE La Trenise. þÿ \\ ear round as before against the sun ; twice box haul the ladv ; range up alongside her, and make sail in company j when half way cross to the other shore, drop astern with the lide short, and cast oil the craft ; now back and fill as iiefore, and box haul her and yourself into jour berth and bring up. FIFTH FIGURE. La Pastorale. þÿ Shoot ahead alongside your partner ; make a stern board and all sail over to the other coast ; let go the hawser, and pay offinto your berth, and take a turn till the three craft opposite range upa-breast twice towards you, and back a stern again ; now manoeuvre any rig you like, only under easysail, as it is always a light breeze, easy zephyrs they call it, in this passage. As soon ns you see their helms down, haul round in company with them on the larboard tack, and make all sail with your partner into your own berth, and bring up. .SIXTH FIGURE. SALT A CURE FOR HYDROPHOBIA. The Rev. J. G. Fischer was formerly a missionary in North America, and is anxious to call the attention of the public to the probable utility of common salt as a remedy in cases of hydrophobia, if at least, the opinion be correct, that what will cure the bites venemous serpents will be edacious in the former class of cases. He says " I actually and effectually cured all kinds of very painful and dangerous serpents' bites, after they had been inflicted for many hours ; for immediately after 1 had applied my remedy, the pain subsided, and the patient calmed þÿ which remedy was nothing else but common table salt ; and I kept it on the place or wound, moistened with Water, till all was healed, within several davs> without ever any bad effect occurring afterwards. I, for my part, never had an opportunity to meet with a mad dog, or any person who was bitten by a mad dog ; I cannot, therefore, speak from experience as to hydrophobia; but that 1 have cured ser|ients' bites, always without fail, 1 can declare in truth " Mr. Fischer then quotes l)r. Urban's ptactice trom Hufeland's General Medical Journal. He had six methods : but his most successful was to apply a thick pledget soaked in any saline solution, to each wound, or to each place where the teeth had made a mark without breaking the skin, and retain them there by bandages. The best solution is of salt, one ounce, or one ounce and a half to a pound of plain water, and the wounds are to be kept constantly moistened with it. The lint is to

be renewed and soaked twice a-day ; the places wetted every two hours, and even washed by the patient, especially if any indications of a relapse, as itching or pain, should manifest themselves. A case is then quoted from the Kent Herald , and Morning Herald , of July 28, 1827, as follows : þÿ " A friend of ours was, some years since, bitten by a dog, which a few hours afterwards died raving mad. Immediately upon receiving the bite, he rubbed salt for some time into the wound, and, in consequence, never experienced the least inconvenience from the bite, the saline qualities of the salt having evidently neutralised the venom, and prevented in all probability a melancholy death by hydrophobia." That which induced Mr. Fischer to try the above remedy, in the case of serpents, was " a page of the late Bishop Loskiel's (with whom 1 was personally acquainted), in his history of Missions of the Moravian Church in North America, which says, as far as I recollect, that at least among some tribes they were not at all alarmed about the bites of serpents, having always in use such a sure remedy as salt for the cure of them þÿ so much so, that they would suffer a bite for the sake of a glass of rum. It was this that 'nduced me to try the cure of venomous bites with salt ; and the trial has exceeded my ex pectations. þÿ P. S. The advice of killing all dogs is neither practicable nor necessary ; apply salt to man and dog, the bitten and biter, all will be most probably well," &c þÿ Journal

of the Royal Institution A French Physician being seized with hydrophobia and entertaining no expectation of recovery went into a vapour bath heated to 42 degrees Reaumur, (120 Fahrenheit,) as the easiest means of suffocation. To his astonishment, the whole symptoms vanished at once, and he has never since had the slightest recurrence of this dreadful disease. By the same means he has cured upwards of eighty patients.

THE SEVEN Bl.r.F.HNa CHRISTIANS. In a volume of sermons by Bishop Heber, he introduces one of the discourses with this story, for the purpose of calling attention to the great concerns of eternity and of practical relitrion. His text is, 2 Cor. iv. 18:" We look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen." þÿ American Baptist and Home Missionary Record There is an ancient fable told by the Greek and Roman Churches, which, fable as it is, may, for its beauty and singularity, well deserve to be remembered. That in one of the earliest persecutions to which the Christian world was exposed, seven Christian youths sought concealment in a lonely cave ; and there, by God's appointment, iell into a deep and death like slumber. They slept, the legend runs, two hundred years, till the greater part of mankind had received the faith of the Gospel, and that Church, which they had left a poor and afflicted orphan, had " kings for her nursing fathers, and queens for her nursing mothers." They then at length awoke, and entering into their native Ephesus, so altered now that its streets were altogether unknown to them, they cautiously inquired il there were any Christians in that city. Christians !" was the answer: " we are all Christians here !" and they heard with thankful joy lhe change which, since they left the world, had taken place in the opinions ot its inhabitants. On one side they were shown a stately fabric, adorned with a gilded cross, and dedicated, as they were told, to the worship of

their crucified Master ; on another, schools for the public expositions of those gospels, of which, so short a tune before, the bare piofession was prescribed and deadly. But no fear was now to be entertained of those miseries which bad encircled the cradle ol Christianity; no danger now of the rack, the lions, or the sword ; the emperor and his perfects held the same faith with themselves, and all the wealth ol the east, and all ihe valor and authority of the western world were exerted to protect and endow the professors and the teachers of their religion. But, joyful as these tidings must at first have been, their further inquiries are said to have met with answers which very deeply surprised and pained them 1 hey learned that the greater part of those who called themselves by the name of Christ were stiangcly regardless of the blessings which Christ hud bestowed, and of the obligations which he had laid on his followers. They found that, as the world had become Christian, Christianity itself had become worldly ; and, wearied and sorrowful, they besought of God to lay them down asleep again, crying out to those who followed them. " You have shown us many Heathen, who have given up their old idolatry, without gaining any thing better in its room ; man)' who are of no religion at all ; and many witli whom the religion of Christ is no more than a cloak of licentiousness ; but where, where are the Christians? And thus they returned to their cave ; At. there God had compassion on them, releasing them, once for all

from that world for whose reproof their days had been lengthened, and removing their souls to the society of their ancient friends and pastors, the martyrs and saints ot an earlier and a better generation. Loveliness. It is not the smiles of a pretty face, nor the tint of the complexion, nor the beauty and symmetry of thy person, nor yet the costly robes and decorations that compose thy artificial beauty ; nor þÿ that enchanting glancef which thou dartest with such lustre on the man thou deignest worthy thy affection. It is thy pleasing deportment, thy chaste onver- c sation, the sensibility and the purity of the thoughts, thy affable and open disposition, sympathising with those in adversity, comforting the afflicted, relieving the distressed, and above all. that humility of soul, that unfeigned and perfect regard of the precepts of Christianity. These virtues constitute thy loveliness. Adorned but with those of nature and simplicity, they shine like the refulgent sun, and display to man that the loveliness of thy person is not to be found in the tinsel ornaments of the body, but >n the reflection of the rectitude and serenity of a well spent life that soars above the transient varieties of this world. þÿ And when thy days are ended here upon earth, thy happy spirit shall be wufted to the regions of eternal bliss.

Caution þÿ A very extraordinary case has occurred in Lincoln of a young man, an assistant to a grocer and tea dealer, who having been in the habit of taking a few leaves of tea in his mouth when weighing that article, imperceptibly introduced so much into his stomach that it hecame an accumulation in the smaller intestines. He was for a long period under medical care, but his ailment could not be discovered. On leaving for the sake of his health, he was better, but, on returning to his employment, he became again indisposed, and suffered great pain, until inflamation produced death. On a post mortem inspection the cause of death was discovered, to the astonishment of his medical attendants; and it is hoped it will be a warning to others not to fall into such a careless habit, which in this case has carried off" in the bloom of his days a remarkably stout and healthy young man. þÿ Stamford Mercury.

From the St. Christopher Gazette , April 21. DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT NEVIS.

It in with deep regret that we announce the intelligence of a disastrous fire that took place on Tuesday night last, in Charlestown, Nevis, which destroyed two-thirds of the Town and levelled to the ground most of the principal houses and all of the Merchants' stores, with property to a considerable amount The fire broke out at about a quarter for 11 o'Cloek, in the premises occupied by Mrs Brown as a hotel, in a room where some cotton was, which bv the carelessness of a bov who entered with alight, ignited, and. before it was discovered or timely assistance could he procured, blazed rapidly, and the destructive element instantly communicated to the adjoining houses. The consternation of the inhabitants mav be better conceived than described, at being awakened in their beds by the appaling cry of fire ! and although numbers rushed to the spot, all the exertions used to prevent the havoc that suc-

TaaiawaasK ceeded, proved fruitless, and the morning's dawn exhibited to the eye a dreadlul scene of devastation. The Editor of this Paper being at Nevis at the time, collected on the next day the following particulars of the number ot houses entirely consumed, and the estimated value of property lost : þÿ South þÿ Mrs Brown's hotel, the property of William Weekes, Esq. The premises occupied as a Custom House. The dwelling and stores ol Mess'rs. Win. Roper & Co., to which was attached the store ot Josiali Nicholson, Esq., A dwelling house occupied by Mr. W. T. Claxton. The premises and stores belonging to Walter M. Mills, Esq.; the dwelling occupied by Miss Gardiner as a hotel. The dwelling and store, the property of Miss Joan Athurton. The large building and store, belonging to

and occupied hv Mr. John Athurton. East þÿ The premises of the late Dr. Caines, (and the lot south ot it.) The dwelling of Miss Ferrier. The itemises and stores of iMess'rs Drew and Matthews þÿ two lots. A new dwelling and store, belonging to G. H. Bans, Esq., The premises and front stores belonging to the heirs of the late Joseph Stanley Esq , occupied bv Mess'rs. Ferrier, Stanley & Co. þÿ The books, money, and most ot the goods were removed to the upper stores in the yard ; their loss is estimated under £400 sterling. The premises and stores of Laurence Nicholson, Esq. To the loss of the above enumerated valuable dwellings, and extensive stores, is to be added that of a considerably quantity ot goods, old wine, and other bottled liquor þÿ lumber, shingles þÿ an immense pile ol boards and other lumber, in the yard of Messrs. W. A Co just landed from a Schooner in the road impossible puncheons of molasses, stored in time for us in the short þÿ fact we had, it was and from the confusion prevailing, to obtain any thing like a correct estimate of the actual value of property in houses, and goods of all descriptions, wiiich has been lost to the town de- nate sufferers. The parts of the unfortustroyed by the fire presents a desolate ap-

þÿpearance arid, we fear, many of the poor houses in some cases, persons þÿ who have sustained the loss ol their their all þÿ will be unable to rebuild them, even to a trifling extent, Bv a rough calculation, in which we were assisted by one or two gentlemen in Nevis, the actual value of the houses and stores destroyed, is stated to be £25,000 ; but to rebuild them, in their former state, would cost nearly double that sum. Of the value of the property in goods, Ac. consumed, no estimate has yet been formed þÿ hut it is supposed to be equal to that of the dwellings and stores. The fire commenced at a quarter before 1 1, and continued to rage, with great violence until 7 o'clock, when the wind changed to the

ATJS. Northward, and drove the flames back to the places that were already burning. The exertions used saved a great" deal of property which was removed to the Church, Parsonage, Court House, Jail, and the private dwellings of Mr Galpine and some other gentlemen. The correspondence in the Post Office, and most of the valuable papers and books in the stores, were saved. The detachment of the 14th Regiment, stationed at the Morning Star, were, by the prompt exertions of their commanding officer Lieut. Grady, soon in town, and with the masters and crews of the vessels in the harbour, rendered great assistance. The exertions of all deserve the highest commendation ; and we cannot refrain from particularizing the conduct of Captain James ilann, master of the drogher sloop Raleigh, of this port, whose exertions were conspicuous His Honor President Daniel, administerng the Government, was at his country seat, but on being informed of the lamentable event, hastened to town early in the morning, when a Privy Council was held. We understood that it was likely that the port of Charlestown would be opened for the importation, free of duties of lumber. An alarm was fired, and the Militia turned out, when Troopers and picquets, were stationed at the different outlets of the town, to prevent the plunder of any property that may have been saved. (Jur fellow Colonists in Nevis have been for some time great sufferers, independently of this recent calamity þÿ A severe drought has long prevailed ; the ground provisions,

which usually constitute the main support of the labouring population, has failed ; supplies of provisions have been so scarce as to render it difficult for some of the Estates to obtain sufficient wherewith to feed the people ; and the short crops, consequent on the long continued dry weather, gave the poor planter but little encouragement to expect better prospects. To the drought, and dreaded famine, was added disease þÿ the Small Box attacked some hundreds, and many cases terminated fatally This lamentable stare of things the fire of Tuesday night has augmented in a ten fold degree ; and the inhabitants of Nevis, generally, and particularly the indigent classes, require not only the sympathy, but the prompt assistance of I heir less unfortunate neighbois. This assistance, we have no doubt, will be both cheerfully and readily afforded, by the other Colonies : a reciprocity of kind feeling and action has always existed, and the inhabitants of the several islands þÿ like one community þÿ have responded to the calls of affliction and humanity, and held out a helping hand to relieve the sufferings of their fellow colonists and fellow beings ? In this Island, we feel pleasure stating, in the strongest feelings of sorrow and sympathy prevail. The extent of the damage sustained in Nevis, w as not known here until a late hour on Wednesday, when some gentlemen left hence for Charleston, to ascertain particulars. At an early hour yesterday morning, a temporary supply of provisions were forwarded, under

the kind charge of the Honourable and Rev, Roper þÿ tor of the Customs. Claxton, I) G. Davis and Robert From the Esq. Collec- exertions made by some gentlemen (who are of the Committee since appointed,) above £200 were obtained in a few hours, by private subscription, and the amount we hope will be greatly increased. Yesterday was the regular day for a meeting of our Legislature; and on the House of Assembly being formed, business was postponed, and a number of the Members repaired to Nevis, with a view of ascertaining the extent of loss, and the manner in which assistance can be best afforded. We understood, from the remarks of several Members, that a grant will be made from the Public Treasury, to be at the disposal of the Committee in Nevis, who may be appointed to .appropriate any sums contributed.

The World. What the world, even to those who love is it ? Who are intoxicated with the pleasures, and who cannot live without it ? The world is a perpetual servitude, where no one lives for himself alone, and where, if we strive to be happy, we must kiss its fetters and love its bondage. The world is a daily revolution of events, which creates in succession, in the minds of its partizans, the most violent passions, bitter hatred, odious perplexities, de-

AT33. vouring jealousy, and grevious chagrins. The world ! it is a place of malediction, where troubles and afflictions. In the world there pleasures themselves carry with them their is nothing lasting þÿ nor fortune the most affluent þÿ nor friendship the most sincere þÿ nor characters the most exalted nor favors the most þÿ enviable. Men pass their lives in agitation, projects and schemes; always ready to deceive, or trying to avoid deception always ; eager and active to profit by the retirement, disgrace or death of their competitors ; always occupied with their lears or their hopes ; always discontented with the present and anxious about the future, never tranquil doing every thing for repose, removing still farther from its vanity, ambition, vengeance, luxury and avarice ; these are the virtues which the world knows and esteems. In the world integrity passes for simplicity ; duplicity and dissimulation are meritorious. Interest the most arms brother against brother, friend and breaks all the ties ot blood and friendship ; and it is this base motive, which produces our hatred and attachments 1 The wants and misfortunes of a neighbor find only indifference and insensibility, whiie we can neglect him without loss, or cannot be recompensed for our assistance. If we could look into two different parts of the world þÿ if we could enter into the secret detail of anxieties and inquietudes þÿ if we could pierce the outward appearance which offers to our eyes only joy, pleasure, pomp, and magnificence,

how different should we find it from what it appears 1 We should see it destitute of happiness þÿ the father at variance with his child ; the husband with his wife; and the antipathies, the jealousies, the murmurs, and the external dissention of his family. We should see friendship broken by suspicions, by caprices ; union the most endearing, dissolved by inconsistency ; relations the most tender, destroyed by hatred and perfidy ; fortunes the most affluent, producing more vexation than happiness ; places the most honorable, not giving satisfaction, but creating desires for higher advancement; each one complaining of his lot, and the most elevated not the most happy.

Something New. We see it announced in one of the Philadelphia papers that Mr. James P. Espy has discovered the laws which govern the weather, and that they are fixed and unalterable. The writer says that

He can inform a captain of a vessel how to tell whether there is a storm raging any where within five hundred miles, of him, and how he must steer to get just as far into the storm as he pleases, and of course have just as much or as little wind as he pleases. He can inform him how always to obtain a supply of pure fresh water at sea þÿ how to ascertain the exact height of the base of a cloud and whether it will he accompanied with violent wind, and how ho must steer if he would avoid it, &c. Verily this Mr. Espy has a most extensivo espionage, and must he on very confidential terms with the clerk of the weather office. He is now lecturing on this new theory at the Franklin Institute, Philadelphia. It reminds us of the alleged discovery of the Frenchman at the Mauritius, who could invariably detect the presence of ships within a few days sail of the Island, from certain appearances in the atmosphere. A DEFENCE OF MARRIAGE. " O, love ol loves ! to thy white hand is gi ven Of earthly happiness the golden key 1" Crosby.

Marriage is the only love lawful. It is the bond which unites the universe Some pretended wise men say the wife is an obstacle to study ; but what hindrance can she be to study who brings to our houses beauty, modesty, and virtue, whocomfoi ts in all the cares, troubles, and mis adventures of life, who consoles us in affliction, who shares our happiness, and who, becoming an inseparable companion of our fortunes, diminishes our ills, and increases our pleasures by the share she has in them ? So far from a wife being a hindrance to study, we might say that she is an inducement to it, because she consoles the weariness that follows it. All the world knows that there is no person exempt from the cares of business. Who can be happier than he who has a wife to console him ? A husband coming out of his study meets with one whose cheerfulness enlivens him after his solitude, whose conversation animates him, and gives new light to his understanding, and who, by the sweetness of her smile, makes him forget the pain the tediousness of study gave him. þÿ Moreover, a wife is not merely a help for study, and a relief to the anxieties which it leaves, but she is also a subject proper for us to study, arid it would not be difficult for us to prove that if a wife be good and virtuous, she produces in her husband's soul a desire of emulation, which induces him to imitate her, and is so far profitable to him that it draws him nearer to the way of virtue than philosophy ilselfean do.
He who finds a wife an obstacle to study, and would banish her from the society of reasonable men, is himself a hindrance to virtue, and to the felicity of mankind.

Nay, indeed, if a wife be of a bad temper, if she is wickedly inclined, sfie constrains us, thereby, to study with care the way to change and mend her. Socrates, the wisest man of antiquity, lived with his wife, Xantippe, whose temper was most unquiet, and as little like an angel's as it is possible for a woman's temper to be ; and, nevertheless, remained so much attached to a wedded life, that no sooner was Xantippe, dead, than be married again, and then gave an illustrious example of the comforts of matrimony. Not only a philosopher, a Socrates, took a wife alter Xantippe but a philosopher who knew by experience the inconvenience of a wicked wife. And Socrates acknowledged for their master. " A virtuous was a philosopher whom other philosophers wife invites to virtue, and a wicked one makes thee exercise it," said that master of antiquity, who suffered with a marvellous tranquillity all the evils inflicted upon him by his wife's temper. It might even be said that a wife is of more advantage to a man than study itself, if we consider the utility of domestic affairs, for how much labor and time should we expend in study before we gain so much as mar riage affords us. What sublunary blessing can raise us to more felicity than a wife's affection ? If we consider the consolation in point of virtue, we find it sublime By the sweetness of that affection we may observe a ray ol the divinity, and our thoughts may be lifted up by beholding the glories of the created to contemplation and admiration and love

of the Creator. What books, what philosophy can teach us the excellence and happiness of virtue, of temperance, moderation, piety, and devotion as the example ol a good wife. If any one should, in reply to these observations, say that all women are not fair, and teat all women are not good, we might say that there is no woman so little gifted with personal charms that custom and conversation may not render fair, nor is there any so wicked whom virtue may not make good. It is the just remark of a modern writer that a woman runs a risk of being spoilt by the flattering period that precedes marriage. She is, of necessity, then, a first object ; and custom has added to the homage which love would willingly render. An individual of a family, who may before have been but little considered, rises at once into importance ; and the person whom she most values is ready to execute the slightest expression of her will. þÿ '1 he sooner that woman can divest herself of any unreasonable expectations which the devotion of the lover may have excited, the greater the probability of her securing permanent attachment. Courtship is a dream, from which it is better to awake voluntarily than to be reluctantly roused, it is better to return to ordinary þÿhabits to the sober and calm fulfilment of daily business, in the place assigned by duly þÿ than to cherish an artificial excitement, and cling to a false position. It is a proof of judgment in a woman, when she bestows attention on her husband's character ;

w hen she sets herself to study his peculiarities, and to consult them to the utmost, of her power This is the management which is not only allowable, but praiseworthy ; for its object is, not the obtaining of sway, but the promotion of mutual felicity. As this, however, is not an essay of the act of married life, we shall conclude our observations by expressing our confidence that a wife is man's best blessing.
