St. Croix, CHRISTIA MS TE I), ( MONDAY ) May 8, 1837. We are much gratified to learn hy advices from Copenhagen to the '25th March, that our beloved King was considered convalescent, and little doubt was entertained at that date, of his Majesty's being soon restored to his usual health.

We learn by the \st April packet from England that a combined movement in advance was made by the Queen's generals in Spain about the middle of March. Espartero entered Durango, the head Quarters o f Don Carlos without much opposition. Saarsfield also advanced on the side of Victoria, but met with little success. Evans on the 1 5th carried the works of the Cat lists in his front, but with heavy loss (800 killed and wounded). On the 18 th he attempted a farther advance on Ilernani, and thj road to Irun, and after several hours fighting, Don Sebastian came up with 12 battalions. completely outflanked Evans division, which was thrown into disorder , and he was only saved hy the steady firmness of the British Royal Marines (regulars,) who stood their ground, and enabled Evans to retreat, with the loss of 2.000 men to St. Sebastians; the result has been that Espartero returned to Bilboa, and each party have resumed their former positions. The bill for the abolition of Church rates has passed the house of Commons ; the numbers being for the bill 273 against it 250

Ministerial majority 23 there is not the least probability of its passing the house of Lords. The death of Viscountess Canning, relict of the celebrated minister, is announced. The title descends to their only son, John Charles Canning, late a member of the house of Commons, and in his 25th year. The weather was remarkably cold in England in March, and the Spring very backward.

From the New York Evening Star, March 6. INAUGURAL ADDRESS. Continued from our last. Certain danger was foretold from the extension of our territory, the multiplication of States, and the increase of population. Our system was supposed to be adapted only to boundaries comparatively narrow. These have been widened beyond conjecture ; the members of our confideracv are already doubled ; and the numbers of our people are incredibly augmented. The alleged causes of danger have long surpassed anticipation, hut none of the consequences have followed. The power and influence of the republic have risen to a height obvious to all mankind ; respect for its authority was not more apparent at its ancient, than it is at its present limits ; new and inexhaustible sources of general prosperity have been opened ; the effects of distance have been averted by the inventive genius of our people, developed and fostered by the spirit of our institutions ; and the enlarged variety and amount of interests, productions, and pursuits, have strengthened the chain of mutual dependance, and formed a circle of mutual benefits, too apparent ever to be overlooked. In justly balancing the powers of the Federal and State authorities, difficulties nearly insurmountable arose at the outset, and subse qucnt collisions were inevitable Amid these, it was scarcely believed possible that a scheme of government, so complex in con. struction, could remain uninjured. From time to time embarrassments have certainly occurred ; but how just is the confidence of future

safety imparted by the knowledge that each in succession has been happily removed. þÿ Overlooking partial and temporary evils as inseparable from the practical operation of all human institutions, and looking only to the general result, every patriot has reason to be satisfied. While the Federal Government has successfully performed its appropriate functions in relation to foreign affairs, and concerns evidently national, that of every State has remarkable improved in protecting and developing local interests and individual welfare, and if the vibrations of authority have occasionally tended too much towards one or the other, it is unquestionably certain that the ultimate operation of the entire system has been to strengthen all the existing institutions, and to elevate our whole country in prosperity and renown. The last perhaps the greatest, of the prominent sources of discord and disaster supposed to lurk in our political condition, was the institution of domestic slavery. Our forefathers were deeply impressed with the delicacy of this subject, and they treated it with a forbearance so evidently wise, that, in spile of every sinister forboding, it never, until the present period, disturbed the tranquility of our common country. Such a result is sufficient evidence of the justice and the patriotism of their course ; it is evidence not to be mistaken that an adherence to it can prevent all embarrassment from this, as well as from every other anticipated cause of difficulty and danger. Have not re-

cent events made it obvious to the slightest reflection, that the least deviation from this spirit ol forbearance is injurious to every interest, that of humanity included ? Amidst the violence pi excited passions, this generous and fraternal feeling has been sometimes dis-

©&sr3K vasimraiiaiR ffisstr-Ksisms AT33» regarded ; and, standing as 1 now do before my countrymen in this high place of honor and of trust, 1 cannot refrain from anxiously invoking my fellow-citizens never to be deaf to its dictates. Perceiving, before my election, the deep interest this subject was beginning excite, to I believed it a solemn duty fully to make known my sentiments in regard to it þÿ and now when every motive for misrepresentation has passed away, I trust that they will be candidly weighed and understood. At least they will be my standard of conduct in the path before me. 1 then declared that, if the desire of those of my countrymen who were favorable to my election was gratified, " 1 must go into the Presidential 'Jhair the inflexible and uncompromising opponent of every attempt, on the part of Congress, to abolish slavery in the District of Columbia, against the wishes of the slaveholding States ; and also with a determination equally decided to resist the slightest interference with it in the States where it exists." 1 submitted also to my fellow citizens, with fulness and frankness the reasons which led me to this determination. The result authorizes me to believe that they have been approved and are confided in, by a majority of the people of the United States, including those whom they most immediately affect. It now only remains to add, that no bill conflicting with these views can ever receive my constitutional sanction. These opinions have been adopted in the firm belief that they are in accordance with

the spirit that actuated the venerated fathers of the republic, and that succeeding experience iias proved them to be humane patriots, expedient, honorable and just. If the agitation of the subject was intended to reach the stability of our institutions, enough has occurred to show that it has signally failed ; and that in this, as in every other instance, the apprehensions of the timid and the hopes of the wicked for the destruction of our government, are again destined to be disappointed. þÿ Here and there, indeed, scenes of dangerous excitement have occurred, terrifying instances of local violence have been witnessed ; and a reckless disregard of the consequences ol their conduct has exposed individuals to popular indignation ; but neither masses of the people, nor sections of the country, have been swerved from their devotion to the bond of union, and the principles it has made sacred it will be ever thus. b>uch attempts at dangerous agitation may periodically return but with each the object will be better understood. That predominating affection for our political system which prevails throughout our territorial limits; that calm and enlightened judg. merit which ultimately governs our people as one vast body ; will always be at band to resist and control every effort, fercign or domestic, which aims, or would lead to overthrow our in- itutions. What can be more gratifying than such a retrospect as this I We look back on obstacles avoided, and dangers overcome; on expecta-

tions more than realized, and prosperity per. fectly secured. To the hopes of the hostile, the fears of the timid, and the doubts of the anxious, actual experience has given the conclusive reply. We have seen time gradually dispel every unfavorable foreboding, and our constitution surmount every adverse circumstance, dreaded at the outset as beyond control. Present excitement will, at all times, magnify present dangers ; but true philosophy

must teach us that none more threatening than the past can remain to be overcome; and we ought, for we have just reason, to entertain an abiding confidence in the stability of our institutions, and an entire conviction that, if administered in the true form, character, and spirit in which they were established, they are abundantly adequate to preserve to us and our children the rich blessings already derived from them ; to make our beloved land, tor a thousand generations, that chosen spot where happiness springs from a perfect equality of political rights. For myself, therefore, I desire to declare, that the principle that will govern me in the high duty to which my country calls me, is, a strict adherence to the letter and spirit of the constitution, as it was designed by those who framed it. Looking back to it as a sacred instrument, carefully and not easily framed; remembering that it was throughout a work of concession and compromise : viewing it as limited to national objects ; regarding it as leaving to the people and the States all power not explicitly parted with; i shall endeavor to preserve, protect, and defend it, by anxiously referring to its provision for direction in every action. To matters of domestic concernment which it has intrusted to the Federal Government and to such as relate to our intercourse with foreign nations, I shall zealously devote myself: beyond those limits I shall never pass. To enter, on this occasion, into a further or more minute exposition of my views on the

various questions of domestic policy would be as obtrusive as it is probably unexpected. þÿ Before the suffrages of my countrymen were conferred upon me, 1 submitted to them, with great precision, my opinions on all the most prominent of these subjects. Our course of foreign policy has been so uniform and intelligible, as to constitute a rule of executive conduct which leaves little to my discretion, unless, indeed, 1 were Swilling to run counter to the lights of experience, and the known opinions of my constituents. We sedulously cultivate the friendship of all nations, as the condition most compatible with our welfare, and the principles of our government. We decline alliances, as adverse to our peace. We desire commercial relations on equal forms, being ever willing to give a fair equiv. alcnt for advantages received. We endeavor to conduct our intercourse with openness and sincerity; promptly avowing our objects, and seeking to establish that mutual frankness which is as beneficial in the dealings of na. tions as of men We have no disposition, and disclaim all right, to meddle in disputes, w hether internal or foreign, that may molest other countries ; regarding them, in their actual state, as social communities, and preserving a strict neutrality in all their controversies. þÿ Well knowing the tried valor of our people, and our exhaustless resources, we neither anticipate nor fear any designed aggression ; and, in the consciousness ol our own just con. duct, we feel a security that we shall never bo

called upon to exert our determination, never to permit an invasion of our rights, without punishment or redress. In approaching, then, in the presence of my assembled countrymen, to make the solemn promise, that yet remains, and to pledge my. self that 1 will faithfully execute the office I am about to fill. I bring with me a settled purpose to maintain the institutions of my country, which, 1 trust, will atone for the errors 1 commit.

Tn receiving from the people the sacred trust twice confided to my illustrious predecessor, and which he has discharged so faith, fully and so well, I know that 1 cannot expect to perform the arduous task with equal ability and success. But, united as 1 have been in his counsels, a daily witness of his exclusive and unsurpassed devotion to his country's welfare, agreeing with him in sentiments which his countrymen have warmly supported, and permitted to partake largely of his confidence, I may hope that somewhat of the same cheering approbation will be found to attend upon my path. For him, I but express, with my own, the wishes of all þÿ that he may yet long have to enjoy the brilliant evening of his well spent life ; and, for myself, conscious of but one desire, faithfully to serve my country, 1 throw myself without fear, on its justice and its kindness. Beyond that, I only look to the gracious protection of the Divine Being, whose strengthening support I humbly solicit, and whom I fervently pray to look down upon us all. May it be among the dispensations of his providence to bless our beloved country with honors and with length of days þÿ may her ways be ways of pleasantness, and all her paths be peace. MARTIN VAN BUREN. Washington, March 4th, 1837.

St. Croix, CIIKISTIA NSTED, ( MUX DA Y) April 3, 1837. It is with much satisfaction we record the fall of a good rain, all over the Island on Thursday afternoon ; it continued upwards of two hours, and it is the fir sit season of rain we have had for several months; þÿ the Island being for some time past in a suffering state, and most of the Cisterns nearly exhausted; and while grateful to an all bountiful Providence for mercies received, we sincerely and fervently pray for a continuance of His favors, in sending us a farther supply of this most necessary blessing. By an extract from the Barbados paper, we perceive the weather there, has been very extraordinary, and we think we have seldom experienced a cooler season, than the one just passed ; particularly the month of March,

From the Barbadian, March 11. The temperature of our atmosphere has been this month of an extraordinary decree of coldness. It is a general remark that the weather during the night, and early in the morning has been colder than ever experienced before in the month of March. We have felt such cold mornings in January and February, but never in March. In the course of the day however the change is rapid. There is scarcely any wind, and the sun is fiercely hot. The day before yesterday the Thermometer in our dressing-room, (having jalousud windows to the East, North, and West), was at J past 4 in the morning at 68 : at past 4 in the afternoon the Mercury had risen to 80 þÿ 12 degrees in 12 hours. Yesterday morning the Thermometer was at 65 at | past 4. The elevation of the mercury as the day advanced was not so groat. This morning at the same hour it was 64. We immersed the Thermometer in a pail of water which had been all night in the open air, and in-half-a minute the mercury fell to 60. The water, when we put our hands into it, caused that almost painful sensation and tingling, which one feels when using cold water in winter. On the country roads the air was keen and bracing, more like a morning of early spring, or late in autumn, than we .should expect to feel in this latitude. Even after sunrise it was very cold 3 or 4 miles out of town. We have had extraordinary high tides this week, and a very rough ground swell on the coast. At Speights' Town we understand the influx of the tide has done some damage. We usually expect high
winds in March ; but, to the great annoyance of our conntiy friends, we hear that the mills cannot work for the want of wind,

It is pleasing to see our harbour so full of merchant ships loading with the produce of our fertile Island. The wharf presents an animated scene of business. An unusually large crop of sugar is expected. We wish we could promise large returns of cash ; but, we have seen discouraging accounts of the probable fall of West India sugar. The extraordinary improvement in the manufacture of East India sugar, and the vast capacity which the extensive regions of the East afford for the production of the cane, with the operation of the equalizing duty, will, it is feared, depress in a serious manner the West India market. Many planters in this Island had, however, are, we understand, very sanguine ; and Es-

The Local Bank of British Guiana has commenced business. This important event was ushered in with great rejoicings in Georgetown. The firing of guns from the vessels in the River of Demerara, announced the suspicious opening of this great money concern. þÿ It will not be long, we trust, before the Colonial Bank will be set going in this Island. A spacious arched vault of solid masonry is now being built at Cavan Hall for the reception of the treasure, which will, we hope, give a fresh spring to commercial and agricultural transactions.

LONDON. (From the Morning Herald, Jan, 24.) The result of the political trials at Strasburg has deprived the guillotine of some intended victims; and whatever disappointment that may cause to the Doctrinaires, it gives us the very opposite feeling to regret. In the pressure of other matter, we have not, however, either time or space to comment upon this subject at present as its importance deserves. As long as there is professedly a Constitutional Government in France þÿ that is, until an absolute Government be avowed and proclaimed, we trust that Juries will make the Monarch feel that the law is not to be used either as a relaxed or well strung bow at his pleasure ; but that it has a certain and defined, and inviolable power, as well as the Royal prerogative.

The preliminary examinations of the affair of Meunier are drawing to a close. Despairing of obtaining any further disclosures from the prisoner, the public authorities are determined to bring forward the trial as soon as possible. Meunier, it is said, answers all the questions, with which he is overwhelmed with the declaration that he had not communicated his project to any one whatever. It was a fatal idea that pursued him every wltere, and which it was impossible for him to resist. It was a demon that instigated liirn. The affair of Meunier w ill probably come forward in the first week of February.
